entities.name: Homeric Hymns
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Homeric Hymns (c. 700–400 BCE) are a collection of 33 ancient Greek religious poems written in the dactylic hexameter of Homeric epic, each addressed to one of the Olympian gods. Though attributed by ancient tradition to Homer, they were composed by various poets across three centuries using Homer's elevated register as the appropriate language for divine praise.

The Hymns range from major narrative poems to brief invocations. The Hymn to Demeter (c. 650 BCE) is among the earliest surviving accounts of Persephone's abduction and the origin of the Eleusinian Mysteries — antiquity's most influential religious institution. The Hymn to Apollo describes his birth on Delos and the founding of his oracle at Delphi. The Hymn to Hermes is a comic masterpiece narrating Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle as a newborn, then inventing the lyre to escape punishment. They were performed at Panhellenic religious festivals as preludes to epic recitations.

The Hymns are primary ancient sources for foundational Greek myths that shaped Western culture. Their characterization of the gods — Apollo as archer-god of reason and music, Aphrodite as irresistible desire, Hermes as clever trickster — defined how Greeks understood divine personality and how Romans, via Ovid and Virgil, transmitted those images to the Renaissance and beyond. The Hymn to Demeter's account of the agricultural cycle and seasonal death-and-rebirth became one of the most analyzed religious texts in classical scholarship, interpreted as the liturgical foundation of Greece's most sacred rites.
